19:15 while the game doesn't use "Real time Ray-Tracing", it uses traditional pre-rendered lighting maps, which are ray-traced, just in advance, so they're not dynamic. In many types of, generally, linear games, this was a perfectly fine technology. You didn't need ray traced global illumination, because the developers have much more control over what see. It limits how many lighting maps they need to render and ship with the game.

In theory it's a much bigger deal for vast open-world games, but we're still quite compute-limited, even today. Thankfully, DLSS4 and FSR4 have changed my opinion on upscalers and have made ray-tracing much more accessible. If you have a 9000-series GPU and haven't checked out Optiscaler, take 5 minutes to check it out, it's the easiest thing to install and enables FSR4 in over 300 games. The ease of install and set-up in game is truly understated.

text:
Please stop using a ring light for your portrait videos. These lamps create a reflection in your eye that appears to be another eye within your eye. Of course, consciously we know that this is not the case, but sub-consciously our brains see it that way, and it makes you look weird: A lizard person from some alien planet. Use a tiny touch of sensitivity and look at your creepy eyes! 
Also the flat lighting makes a person's face look flat. You need to have more light on one side to get chiaroscuro; that is, a sense of 3D relief created by highlights and shadows. 
As a former professional portrait photographer. I am giving you informed advice. Seek to get your facial skin tones to occupy the range from 80% (highlights) to 20% (shadows). This will make it possible to have skin tones throughout without parts blowing out to saturated white or collapsing to solid black. This recommended range is the linear (or near linear) range of digital sensors, much the same as it was with film, in the day. You can achieve this with a large square diffuser light source to the side of the camera, and light walls in your recording studio. The reflection of you diffuser lamp will appear to be a window in your eyes, and the human brain is accustomed to reading this reflection without disturbing effects. 
The ring lamp is perfect to close up shots of things like mother boards, postage stamps, coins and small items of jewelry. But never faces.

text: @TheBrawlingBrothers  Its the opposite as far as CPU bottlnecking that is.   In other words with higher resolutions the bottlenck shifts to the GPU while lower resolutions shift to the CPU as the bottleneck.   The reason for this is the CPU feeds the GPU the iformation to generate the frames.  At lower resolutions the GPU dosnt work as hard and can pump out tons of frames supper fast but the CPU cant keep up with the GPU.   But at higher resolutions the GPU cant generate teh frames as fast its under a heavier workload which makes it easier for the CPu to keep up.   So a 9800x3d wont help you with 4k gaming like at all.   However a 9800x3d might hep a little with 1440p if you have a high end gpu like a 5080 or 5090.  Now at 1080p is where the 9800x3d will show a decent improvement over say the 9700x.   Basically the 9800x is best for those that want max frames at lower resolutions.    If you like your game looking pretty with high graphics settings then there will be very little diffrence between any of the ryzen CPUs.
